claims.text: Annealing near the alloy's order-disorder transition followed by rapid quenching will create nanoscale precipitates.
The anneal-quench treatment will refine grain boundaries.
Nanoscale precipitates and refined grain boundaries will pin magnetic domain walls.
Domain-wall pinning will require a larger applied field to reverse magnetization and therefore increase coercivity.
Standard melting and casting of the proposed equimolar magnetic high-entropy alloy yields a random solid solution with a relatively coarse, homogeneous microstructure.
A treatment at approximately 600–700°C for 1 hour followed by water or oil quenching is the proposed intervention.
Rapid quenching will freeze in the microstructural changes generated during annealing.
The annealed and quenched sample will have a higher coercive field than a composition-matched conventionally melted and cast sample.
The conventionally processed baseline has fewer domain-wall-pinning features than the treated sample is expected to have.
The predicted coercivity increase depends on the alloy permitting formation of suitably sized precipitates.
Overaging or processing conditions that prevent suitable precipitate formation may eliminate the predicted coercivity increase.
The effect is to be tested at room temperature under quasi-static magnetic-hysteresis measurement conditions after treatment in an inert atmosphere or controlled vacuum.
The optimal annealing temperature, duration, and quench rate, and the sensitivity of coercivity to those parameters, remain uncertain.
